title: Backed Unitree but missed the follow-on: even patient capital gets stuck by fund cycles
dek: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but in the 2023 round it couldn't follow on because its own USD fund was expiring and it was raising a new one. Doubling down tests not just vision but the match between fund and project timing.
why: A person who has done 17 years of hard-tech VC inside Singapore's sovereign capital system lays out the betting logic on chips, robotics and low-altitude economy, and candidly reviews why he missed ByteDance and the Unitree follow-on.
who: For founders and investors focused on hard tech, robotics and the raise-invest-manage-exit cycle of USD funds, especially those who want to know how a sovereign-backed VC makes independent judgments and how it reviews missed follow-ons.
skip: 27:35 to 33:28 covers Singapore clan associations, the Zhongyuan Festival and Chinese cohesion, which is weakly related to investment judgment.

points.h: They started investing when chips were cheaper than potato chips
points.body: Vertex invested in semiconductors as early as 2011 and in a solid-state battery materials company in 2012, when almost no domestic VC would look at them because the internet was at its peak. Zheng Juncong told a joke: chips are called chips, and everyone thought a chip was cheaper than a potato chip, so nobody invested, because chips were imported and sold for only one US dollar each. He judged that chips had extremely high technical content, from millions of lines of code to billions of lines of code, and that all electronic products, cars and the cloud would need them. The pitch for investing in chips also changed with the times: first it was domestic production being tax-exempt, then iterating around the mobile phone supply chain, and now it is being bottlenecked plus next-generation applications like optical computing.

points.h: The IC can pass by half, and there is a golden share
points.body: Vertex's investment committee does not need a unanimous vote, only a majority, and it will even convene on weekends if a project needs to go to IC. More unusual is the golden share: a partner has one chance a year to force an investment in a company even if the IC did not approve it. Votes are secret; you do not know whether a partner voted yes or no, because they do not want everyone to go easy on each other and give up independent judgment. The vote choice is also tied to project outcomes over the long term: if a project fails but you voted yes, it is traced back into your score, and when carry is distributed it is brought out to look at. This mechanism is designed to force independent judgment, not votes based on personal ties.

points.h: They don't chase hype, because founders of fought-over deals get cocky
points.body: Vertex explicitly does not invest in projects that are especially sought after in the market. Zheng Juncong gives two reasons: first, everyone fighting over it drives up the valuation; second, when a founder is fought over, he focuses on valuation and feels investors are all flattering him, so he will not keep his feet on the ground building the company, and the success rate is actually lower. They value founders who do solid technology, have patience, want to create value, and do not rely on publicity. They have zero tolerance for financial fraud, because Singapore cares a lot about integrity and truthfulness, and once fraud is discovered they will definitely exit. This style also explains why they did not invest in many money-burning internet companies.

points.h: Given another chance on large models, they still wouldn't invest, because it's like the internet
points.body: Over the past four years the undisputed hot spot for Chinese investment has been AI large models, and Vertex did not make a move in the first three or four years, which is very unusual among first-tier funds. Zheng Juncong's reasoning: large-model startups in China have no advantage; the advantage will come from customers, data and application scenarios, and it requires being big enough and able to burn a lot of money; it is essentially an internet playbook, and the business model is still unclear. The two biggest internal camps were "this will definitely take off, China will definitely have large models" and "model risk is high, it may keep burning money like the internet, and existing large internet companies have a higher probability of success." He admits this discourages young investors who want to participate, but they held back because they firmly believe hard tech is the advantage.

points.h: Singapore certification: swap the chip, swap the software, then export
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Singapore can help Chinese entrepreneurs solve two things: product internationalization and product security. Products made with China's manufacturing, design and innovation capabilities are wanted worldwide, but when they run into geopolitics, politicians will obstruct them on the grounds that "Chinese products are unsafe, robots might carry things and run around hitting people on the street." Singapore, as a neutral, transparent country with a good reputation, can achieve "Citified by Singapore" — the chip is certified here, or swapped for a chip made here and software made here, and then exported from here, allowing the product to enter other countries. He also criticizes "Singapore Washing": companies that move here only to slap on a label, with no actual operations or R&D, are the term he least wants to hear.

points.h: Boston Dynamics cost over $100k; Wang Xingxing sold for just over $10k
points.body: In 2019 Zheng Juncong went to Boston for a board meeting and visited Boston Dynamics, wanting to buy a robot dog. They said they would not sell, and the cost was about over one hundred thousand US dollars. After returning to China he judged that China is strong at hardware and someone must be doing it, so he had his team search all Chinese robotics teams and found Wang Xingxing. At the time the robot dog was already very agile, able to stand up and bow. He asked whether it was controlled by AI, and Wang Xingxing said no, it used his own algorithm. Asked about cost, Wang Xingxing did not mention cost, only said it currently sold for about just over ten thousand US dollars. The same dog cost others over one hundred thousand, and he sold it for just over ten thousand; Zheng Juncong judged there was commercialization potential, and cost is a very important element in technological innovation.

points.h: Missed the Unitree follow-on: fund expired, not enough bullets
points.body: Vertex was the sole institutional investor in Unitree's Pre-A+ round in 2020, but the follow-on only came in September 2024, when Unitree had already produced the G1 bipedal robot and its valuation had soared. Why not follow on earlier? Zheng Juncong reviews: when they invested, they saw a market of several billion, not that bipedal robots could be built; in the 2023 round, Matrix Partners and Shunwei came in, and they also wanted to invest, but their own USD fund was just at the end of its term and they were raising a new fund, so they did not have enough bullets to add to their position, and they missed that round. He calls it a very big regret, and says this made them reflect; now the new fund requires starting to raise new money once 65% is invested, reserving 20% to 30% for follow-ons.

points.h: Wang Xingxing raised slowly, but that forged mass-production consistency
points.body: Zheng Juncong believes Wang Xingxing does not need to be better at fundraising; the current fundraising pace is actually the best. If back then he had been very good at fundraising and raised a lot of money in the next round, the playbook might have been different — flashy, more money-burning, no discipline in running the company, not nitpicking cost details, and the models produced might not be profitable. After AI arrived, many companies want to copy Unitree, thinking the barrier is not high, it is just algorithms, and they can catch up quickly with AI. Zheng Juncong says everyone can get algorithms to roughly the same level, but the real gap is mass production and consistency, which is built up from all past investment and time, and no second company on the market has his mass-production consistency.

points.h: A crude way to judge a bubble: look at who is starting companies
points.body: Asked whether China's embodied intelligence has a bubble, Zheng Juncong says no, because the market is still expanding and in its creation phase. He gives a rough indicator for judging a bubble: when the entrepreneurs you attract are not real entrepreneurs but people who were at big companies without entrepreneurial spirit, who see others succeed and raise money and jump out saying they want to start a company too, that is the point when a bubble appears. Right now the entrepreneurs he sees are all "I am a doer" types, very strong and capable people. He quotes Lee Kuan Yew saying the market needs bubbles, like beer is not tasty without foam, but too much foam is also not good, and it should be controlled at an appropriate proportion.

terms.def: Vertex's investment committee mechanism: a partner can, once a year, force an investment in a project that the IC rejected.
Distributions to paid-in capital: the money LPs actually get back divided by the capital invested, the hardest metric sovereign funds use to assess GPs.
When a Chinese company only slaps a label on a Singapore headquarters without actual operations or R&D.
Electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, the core category of the low-altitude economy, using multiple electric rotors instead of a helicopter's single engine.
Using AI to research new materials, chemical structures and other problems humans cannot calculate.
